what_it_does: Modern processors run faster by 'prefetching' — secretly fetching the next instructions before they are actually needed, like a librarian pulling the next chapter before you finish the current one. This prefetching relies on a small lookup table called the Branch Target Buffer (BTB) that records where each 'branch' instruction (a point in the code that can jump to different locations) will jump next; but this table is small and when entries are evicted (removed to make room), future prefetches for those branches fail or go to the wrong place, hurting performance especially for large server programs with many code paths. Skia introduces 'shadow branches' — lightweight placeholders that stay in a separate, larger table after a full BTB entry is evicted, recording just enough information (the branch's address and its destination) to keep the prefetcher pointed in the right direction without the overhead of keeping the full BTB entry alive. This prevents the processor's front-end from stalling or fetching the wrong instructions without significantly enlarging the expensive BTB itself.
